courseTitle: Physics 2: Fluids, Heat, Electricity, Light and Atoms
title: Electric Potential and Voltage
short: Potential is energy per charge, V = kq/r near a point charge, and a charge crossing ΔV gains or loses qΔV of kinetic energy.
trouble: Students mix up potential (a scalar, energy per charge) with potential energy or with the field.

blocks.html: The potential energy of a charge depends on that charge. Divide it out, just as we did to get the electric field from the force, and you get a property of the place itself: the electric potential, measured in volts.

If a charge $q$ at some point has potential energy $U$, then $V = U/q$ is the energy each coulomb would have there. Near a point charge, $U = kQq/r$, so $V = kQ/r$. Potential is a scalar, so for several charges you just add numbers, signs included. When a charge moves between two points, its potential energy changes by $q\Delta V$; if only electric forces act, its kinetic energy changes by the opposite amount.

$V = \dfrac{U}{q}$, in volts ($1\,\text{V} = 1\,\text{J/C}$). Near a point charge, $V = k\dfrac{Q}{r}$. A charge crossing a potential difference $\Delta V$ has $\Delta U = q\Delta V$ and $\Delta K = -q\Delta V$. One electron volt, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$, is the energy an electron gains crossing $1\,\text{V}$.

blocks.title: Near a point charge
blocks.q: Find the potential $0.30\,\text{m}$ from a $+6.0\,\text{nC}$ charge.

blocks.title: Two charges
blocks.q: A $+4.0\,\text{nC}$ charge is at $x = 0$ and a $-2.0\,\text{nC}$ charge at $x = 0.40\,\text{m}$. Find the potential at $x = 0.20\,\text{m}$.

blocks.title: An electron gun
blocks.q: An electron starts from rest and crosses a potential difference of $1000\,\text{V}$. Find its kinetic energy and speed.
steps: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(1.60 \times 10^{-16})}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}} = 1.87 \times 10^{7}\,\text{m/s}$, about 6% of the speed of light.

blocks.html: Mixing up potential with potential energy, or with the field. Potential $V$ is energy per coulomb and a scalar; potential energy $U = qV$ depends on the charge; the field $\vec E$ is a vector and depends on how $V$ changes from place to place. Check the units: volts, joules, or newtons per coulomb.
